Heliocentrism. The astronomical model placing the Sun at the center of the cosmos with Earth and other planets orbiting it. A radical departure from the Earth-centered Ptolemaic system that had dominated astronomy for nearly two millennia. Proposed in its modern form by Copernicus in fifteen-forty-three and vindicated observationally by Galileo in sixteen-ten and explained dynamically by Newton in sixteen-eighty-seven. Heliocentrism was both a scientific revolution and a cultural earthquake, challenging religious orthodoxy and forcing a reckoning between faith and empirical observation.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the second century CE, developed the geocentric model with Earth at the center and the Sun orbiting it. This system was mathematized with epicycles, or circles on circles, to match observations and dominated astronomy for fourteen hundred years. Nicolaus Copernicus published De revolutionibus orbium coelestium in fifteen-forty-three, proposing the Sun at the center. His heliocentric model was mathematically simpler and more elegant than Ptolemy's but faced immediate resistance from the Church.

Galileo Galilei, in sixteen-ten, used the telescope to observe Jupiter's moons, sunspots, and lunar mountains. Phenomena incompatible with Ptolemaic theory, they provided observational evidence for heliocentrism and drew Church condemnation. Isaac Newton, in sixteen-eighty-seven, explained why heliocentrism works. His laws of motion and universal gravitation show that the Sun's gravity dominates the solar system and planets must orbit it elliptically, following Kepler's laws.

The shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism symbolized the Scientific Revolution. The replacement of authority, whether Aristotle or the Church, with observation and mathematics as the arbiter of truth. Heliocentrism displaced humanity from the center of the cosmos, a psychological blow known as the Copernican principle. Yet paradoxically it enabled deeper understanding of Earth's place in an infinite universe.

Retrograde motion puzzled ancient astronomers. Mars and other planets appear to reverse direction in the night sky for weeks, then resume forward motion. Ptolemy explained this with epicycles. Copernicus explained it simply: Earth overtakes the outer planets. The shift required not just heliocentrism but also elliptical orbits. Kepler, in the early sixteen-hundreds, showed planets orbit ellipses, not circles. Copernicus still clung to circular orbits, explaining some discrepancies with observations.

Heliocentrism sparked the Scientific Revolution itself. It placed humanity on a moving planet orbiting an ordinary star. This psychological shift, the Copernican principle, remains one of science's most humbling ideas.
